layout_dets.text: THE DISSOLUTION AND PASSIVATION KINETICS OF

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: STAINLESS ALLOYS CONTAINING MOLYBDENUM—II.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: DISSOLUTION KINETICS IN ARTIFICIAL PITS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: R. C. NEWMAN*

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Department of Applied Science, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY 11973, U.S.A.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract—Artificial pit electrodes of Fe-Cr-Ni and Fe-Cr-Ni-Mo alloys have been polarized in a neutral

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1M KCl solution at 22°C. The active dissolution kinetics in the nearly saturated pit environments have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been determined; 1.6 at.% Mo depresses the anodic dissolution rate in the active region by a factor of 5–10,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: depending on the potential. The consequent displacement of the corrosion potential in the pit is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approximately the same as the change in pitting potential caused by the molybdenum addition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experiments with 0.0065M sodium thiosulphate added to the bulk solution indicate that the alloy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing molybdenum is considerably less sensitive to the activating effect of adsorbed sulphur.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In PART I we examined the mechanism of the molybdenum effect on active dissolution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Fe-Cr alloys. Part II deals with the effect of molybdenum on active dissolution in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simulated pits. In these experiments an alloy containing nickel has been used, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuity with earlier artificial pit studies.1,2 The effects of molybdenum additions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are quite similar in Fe-Cr and Fe-Cr-Ni alloys.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is well known that molybdenum at 0.5–4 at.% raises the pitting potential and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: crevice corrosion resistance of stainless steels in chloride solutions. Very resistant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nickel-based alloys are also produced commercially with molybdenum concentra-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tions as high as 17 wt% (11 at.%). Many attempts have been made to explain the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beneficial effect of molybdenum, and these have been reviewed by Wanklyn.³ Some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the relevant experimental evidence is listed below:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (1) Molybdenum is effective in conjunction with chromium. It inhibits active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissolution in acidic solutions and is enriched with chromium on the active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surface.⁴

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (2) The inhibiting effect of molybdenum on active dissolution is more pro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nounced in mildly acidic solutions (pH ≥ 0.5) than in more concentrated ones

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (3) Molybdenum usually has a small effect on the potential of the IR-corrected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anodic current maximum, whereas this is the main effect of chromium.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (4) Molybdenum is usually depleted in well-established passive films, though it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is almost always detected.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (5) Additions of molybdate ions to the solution have an inhibiting effect similar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to that of molybdenum in the alloy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Observation (5) has led to suggestions tha the inhibiting species in molybdenum-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing alloys is a form of precipitated iron molybdate (e.g. reference 5).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: However, this seems inconsistent with the kinetics of the pit initiation process, since

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reaction (if it can occur at all) must be several orders of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: magnitude slower than the other anodic processes which can occur at a pit nucleus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where active dissolution has initiated. The situation may be different in a more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advanced stage of pit growth or after pit repassivation; evidence for molybdenum-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rich material in pits has been obtained by Kodama and Ambrose6 and recently by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Moriya and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using a Ni-Mo alloy and an elegant microscopic technique. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likelihood of forming solid molybdenum compounds depends on the molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content of the alloy, the presence of chromium (because of the low pH of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions), the potential of pit growth and the presence of anions other than chloride.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The Moriya and Ives experiment is subject to all these reservations, since they used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high-Mo, Cr-free alloys, a rather high potential of 0.5 V(SCE) and had a sulphate to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chloride ratio of 15:1.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One can express the inhibiting effect of molybdenum in terms of the change in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting resistance per wt.% of molybdenum (e.g. critical pitting temperature). In this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: way the pitting behaviour of a number of different alloys can be rationalized.8 The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improvement which molybdenum imparts to a relatively susceptible Fe-Cr alloy is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparable with the improvement in a more highly alloyed material with about the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same chromium content. However, there does seem to be a relationship between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chromium content and the effectiveness of small molybdenum additions.º At around

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 25% chromium, strong inhibition of pitting results from the addition of only about

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1 wt.% Mo. All these observations are significant in assessing models of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum effect which involve high oxidation states—for example, if molybdates

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were involved one would expect them to be produced at the high potentials on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resistant alloys, but not at the much lower potentials on the more susceptible alloys.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nevertheless, molybdenum is effective in alloys with quite low pitting potentials,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including those examined in this paper. If one regards the molybdenum effect on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting potential as an effect of enriched elemental molybdenum on the active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissolution kinetics,4,1º then it is not surprising that molybdenum has a comparable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effect on a variety of different alloys. The stronger effect of molybdenum at high

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chromium concentrations9 might be due to a reduced number of surface

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heterogeneities which must become enriched in molybdenum by preferential dissolu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion of iron. In general, the role of chromium is to passivate the alloy, and that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum is to inhibit active dissolution. Wanklyn³ showed that it was unlikely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that molybdates were responsible for the resistance to crevice corrosion introduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by molybdenum, but did not commit himself firmly on the role of molybdenum in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting at high' potentials. His argument was essentially thermodynamic; we include

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 1 to indicate the relative stability of various species in non-complexing solutions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One should bear in mind that the pH of the saturated pit solution is less than 0.5.²

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The present work aims to understand the pitting dissolution of an Fe-Cr-Ni-Mo

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloy in a neutral chloride solution. For this purpose a uniform pitting dissolution is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: established at the bottom of an artificial pit. The kinetics are compared with those of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an Fe-Cr-Ni alloy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: EXPERIMENTAL METHOD

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: High purity Fe-Cr-Ni and Fe-Cr-Ni-Mo alloys (Table 1) were melted as small ingots and drawn into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1 mm wire with several intermediate anneals. Small coupons were also prepared by hot rolling. The wires

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were abraded, annealed at 1200°C for 24 h and water quenched. They were then mounted in rods of epoxy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resin to make lead-in-pencil' electrodes'² as shown in Fig. 2. An initial depth of 1 mm was established by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: again because that would require a supersaturation of the solution."Active dissolution was allowed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proceed at this rate for 1000 s to make sure that the system was in a steady state. The solution resistance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was measured using an imposed 1 MHz ac current; the true (IR-corrected) potentials during active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissolution at 90 mA/cm² were -170 and –110 mV for Fe-Cr-Ni and Fe-Cr-Ni-Mo respectively.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To measure the active dissolution kinetics in the pit solution, the potential was progressively stepped

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to more negative values with intermediate periods at the original value between 0 and 100 mV (Fig. 3).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The hold time at the original value was 14 s and the time at each of the more negative potentials was 7 s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The current after 5 s at each potential was used to plot E-log icurves. The solution resistance was measured

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the beginning and end of this procedure, and an averaged value was used to apply an IR correction to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the E-log i curves. The decrease in metal ion concentration at the pit bottom resulting from the 5 s delay

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at each potential was estimated as 2% .1.2

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In one set of experiments the effect of sulphur impurities was studied by adding 1 g/l (0.0065M) of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sodium thiosulphate to the 1M KCl solution. Thiosulphate is known to enhance the pitting of stainless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloys³ and acts through an adsorbed sulphur layer on the metal surface.

layout_dets.text: The artificial pit experiments typically produced data like those shown in Fig. 4.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The IR corrections were large and R varied slowly with time, necessitating several

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experiments because of the inevitable scatter in the corrected data. Some earlier

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results on the Fe-Cr-Ni alloy were slightly overcorrected.1.2 The anodic ‘Tafel slope

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perturbations caused by the multiple potential pulsing method.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 5 gives the results of two artificial pit experiments on each alloy. In the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linear portion above about 1 mA/cm², molybdenum reduces the current density at a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: given potential by a factor of about five. The consequent displacement of the ‘Tafel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: line' on the potential axis is about 60 mV. The difference between the corrosion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentials in the pit solutions is larger (about 130 mV). Very similar polarization

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curves, not shown, were obtained for flat coupon electrodes in acidic solutions such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as 4M HCl. The inhibiting effects of molybdenum are tabulated in Table 2, showing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that its effect in the pit solution is less than in 1M HCl but similar to that found in 4M

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: HCl. The effect of molybdenum is also very similar to its effect in Fe-Cr alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (reference 9, Fig. 1). The main difference between the Fe-Cr and Fe-Cr-Ni alloys is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a shift of the active region by about +150 mV; this is due to surface enrichment of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nickel.14 In many ways, the effects of nickel and molybdenum are similar except that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: containing about 1M of metal ions in a defect (such as a crack in the passive film)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: about 10 nm in depth.15 This suggests that the defects which initiate pitting are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diffusionally equivalent to at least a 1 μm-deep cavity. Such a cavity could be a crack

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The effects of sulphur compounds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 6 reproduces the data of Fig. 5 as schematic straight lines, and adds the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data obtained with 0.0065M sodium thiosulphate added to the 1M KCl. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fe-Cr-Ni alloy showed a spectacular acceleration of anodic dissolution by more than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an order of magnitude; the salt film could be maintained at (IR corrected) potentials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as low as -250 mV. The acceleration was much less marked on the Fe-Cr-Ni–Mo

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloy, where it amounted to a factor of 3–7, depending on the potential. These data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be explained in several ways, and more work is needed. The following hypothesis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seems consistent with the available facts:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (1) The anodic dissolution of the Fe-Cr-Ni alloy is controlled by a surface nickel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: monolayer (or sub-monolayer) which like pure nickel is very sensitive to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sulphur adsorption.14,18 The consequent acceleration of nickel dissolution by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sulphur makes the alloy behave very much like a nickel-free alloy in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sulphur-free solution (reference 10, Fig. 1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (2) The dissolution of the Fe-Cr-Ni-Mo alloy is controlled by molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: atoms enriched at critical sites10,19which are not as sensitive as nickel atoms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to sulphur adsorption.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (3) Alternatively (or simultaneously) the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ion may react with adsorbed or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissolved sulphur species and reduce their availability for adsorption on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surface nickel atoms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is well known that austenitic stainless steels, containing nickel, pit almost exclu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sively at sulphide inclusions, whereas ferritic steels pit more randomly and can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Kinetics of stainless alloys containing molybdenum—II.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tested for pitting using a scratch test.2º If one assigns a chemical role to the sulphide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inclusions (e.g. forming

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which accelerates metal dissolution by adsorption), then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the presence of nickel (which is especially sensitive to sulphur) will make the alloy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more sensitive to the presence of the inclusions because the dissolution rate of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloy is controlled by nickel. From the present results we can speculate that alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing molybdenum, which are less sensitive to sulphur impurities, will also have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: less preference (other things being equal) for sulphide inclusions as pitting sites. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: earlier work on the effects of sulphur compounds on pitting³ it was observed in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passing (last paragraph) that thiosulphate ions did not have much effect on materials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more highly alloyed than Type 304 stainless steel. It was speculated that thiosulphate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would not be reduced to adsorbed sulphur at the higher potentials required to pit the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more resistant alloys. However, since the more resistant alloys contained molyb-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denum, it is also possible that the sulphur (though present in its active form) was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: being rendered harmless by the molybdenum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Additional comments and conclusions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The understanding of the effects of molybdenum which we have gained in this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: work will now be summarized. First, there was nothing unusual or grossly time-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dependent about the behaviour of the Mo-containing alloy in the artificial pit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experiments. It maintained a steady active state or could become salt-covered at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher potentials. Although its active dissolution could not be studied at the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential (because of salt precipitation) there is no reason to suppose that important

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: new anodic processes (except slow

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formation) would occur in the 150 mV

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the pitting potential and the highest potential examined. It is most unlikely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that molybdates are involved in the pitting of alloys at these relatively low potentials,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: although

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be important in an advanced stage of pitting. Nevertheless,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum exerted a strong inhibiting effect on pitting which was closely related to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its 5-10 times reduction of the anodic kinetics in the pit environment. It can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concluded that both pit initiation and pit propagation are related to the inhibition of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: active dissolution by submonolayer surface enrichment of molybdenum.10,18 In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addition, some evidence was obtained that molybdenum mitigates the activating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effect of sulphur compounds on pitting dissolution. Future work should aim to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: understand the co-operative behaviour of chromium and molybdenum, and will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involve measurement of dissolution and passivation in solutions of less than the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: saturated metal ion concentration, since this is where chromium exerts its effect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Artificial pit studies of the roles of copper, tungsten and nitrogen are also in progress.
